title: Even or Odd
story: You're sorting a big pile of socks into pairs. Every time you find two matching socks, you make a pair and put them aside. But what if there's a leftover sock without a partner? That leftover means you have an odd number. Let's teach your program to figure out if any number is even or odd!
why: The modulo operator `%` is one of the most useful math tools in programming. It tells you what's left over after division, which helps with everything from alternating colors in a game to checking if a number is divisible.
analogy: The modulo `%` is like dealing cards to friends — after dealing evenly around the circle, the cards left in your hand are the remainder.
try_it: Test numbers 1 through 10 with your even/odd checker. Which numbers are even? Can you modify the program to print 'Divisible by 3!' if the number is divisible by 3 instead? (Hint: use `number % 3 == 0`.)
tips: `%` gives the remainder after division: `7 % 2` is 1 because 7 = 3×2 + 1.
When `number % 2 == 0`, the number is even. When `number % 2 == 1`, it's odd.
You can use `%` with any divisor: `% 3` checks divisibility by 3, `% 5` by 5, and so on.
The modulo operator works on both positive and negative numbers.
common_mistakes: Using `/` instead of `%`: `7 / 2` gives 3 (the quotient), `7 % 2` gives 1 (the remainder).
Writing `number % 2 = 0` instead of `number % 2 == 0` — use double equals for comparison.
Forgetting parentheses: `number % 2 == 0` is correct; `number % 2 = = 0` with spaces in the double equals won't work.
